BJT DC Bias II: Finding the State, β Sensitivity, Other Configurations and Design

Why this matters in the exam: BJT DC analysis is worth 22 of the 50 marks on the practice test: Q6 (load line, 6 marks), Q7 (Thevenin at the base plus the active-mode model, 10 marks) and Q8 (two transistors, one of them pnp, 6 marks). Workshop 5, Sections 4 to 6, is built around the guess, analyse, check loop, β ranges and bias design. The test reuses workshop questions verbatim. Expect at least one question where the first guess (active) is wrong, and one with a pnp or a second transistor.

E4 covered the three modes, fixed bias, emitter bias, voltage-divider bias and the load line. This pack covers everything that comes up once those are solid.

1. The core ideas

1.1 The three large-signal models (WS5 Section 4)

State Replace the BJT with What you know What you must find to check Check passes if
Active 0.7 V source B to E, plus a current source from C to E , , and and V
Saturation 0.7 V source B to E, plus a 0.2 V source C to E , and (separately) , and
Cut-off Open circuit at all three terminals V
  • Use: every DC question where the state is not given, and as the final line of every question where it is.
  • Trap: in saturation . That relation is the active-mode model. In saturation the collector current is set by the external circuit, and (the “forced β”) is less than β.

1.2 What a failed check tells you

Active-mode result Meaning Next guess
V, often negative The collector circuit cannot carry Saturation
(or ) The base-emitter junction is not forward biased Cut-off

A negative is not an arithmetic slip. It is the standard sign that the transistor is saturated (WS5 Q10, Q12).

1.3 β sensitivity

The active-mode base loop for any single-transistor bias circuit has this form:

  • If , then , which does not depend on β. This is why emitter and voltage-divider bias are stable.
  • If (fixed bias), . Doubling β doubles .
  • Worst cases. gives the largest and the smallest , so check it to avoid saturation. gives the smallest , so check it to guarantee saturation (WS5 Q12, Q13) or to guarantee a minimum current.
  • Trap: with a β range, work both ends and quote both answers (WS5 Q16).

These are the New Q3 values with = 560 Ω. Slide β from 200 down to 100 and watch how far the Q-point moves; then set to 0 and repeat.

1.5 pnp sign conventions

Everything is a mirror image of the npn case:

npn pnp
Active base-emitter V (base above emitter) V (emitter above base)
Current directions in, in, out out, out, in
Active check V V
Typical supply at the collector at the emitter, or the collector to a negative rail

Method: work in magnitudes (, ). Draw the actual current arrows on the circuit before writing KVL, and write every drop as (current in the arrow direction) × R. The relations , and are unchanged.

1.6 Two-transistor direct-coupled DC (Week 5 slides 84 to 88)

  • There is no capacitor between the stages, so stage 1’s DC levels are stage 2’s bias.
  • Order: solve stage 1’s base loop. That gives , which sets the node joined to stage 2 (usually ). Then go through stage 2.
  • Base-current loading: the node also carries . For an npn second stage, is drawn from , so carries . For a pnp second stage, flows into the node, so carries . The lecture example ignores . Say so if you do the same.
  • Diode-connected transistor (base tied to collector, as in practice test Q8): , so it is always active and simply drops one .

1.7 Bias design (Week 4 slides 48 to 51, WS5 Section 6)

Design is analysis run backwards: you know the target currents and voltages, so each unknown resistor is . Rules of thumb for voltage-divider bias (Boylestad Ch. 4):

Choice Rule Why
Large enough to stabilise , small enough to leave room for
From the collector loop
Makes the approximate method valid, so does not depend on β
, with Divider with the base current neglected

Finish by choosing standard values and re-analysing with the exact method to show that the target is still met.

1.8 The Early effect (Week 4 slides 9 to 11; WS5 Q1)

In real devices the active-region curves slope upward. If you extend them backwards, they meet at . As rises, the collector-base depletion region widens and the effective base width shrinks, so and rise. This is called base-width modulation.

  • Use: appears in small-signal models (E6). For DC work, ignore it unless the question gives .
  • Example: = 100 V and = 1 mA give 100 kΩ. At = 5 V, is 5 % above the value with the Early effect ignored.
  • Trap: a steeper slope means a smaller , which is less ideal.

2. The method

2.1 Recognising the question type

Wording or feature Type Playbook
“find the operating mode / state”, no state given State determination A
“assume active” Analysis plus a one-line check A (step 4 only)
“”, “minimum and maximum β”, “always saturated” Sensitivity B
A resistor from collector to base Collector feedback A with the loop
Collector at a rail, output at the emitter Emitter follower A
Base grounded, signal into the emitter Common base A, emitter loop first
An arrow into the emitter, , or negative rails pnp C
Two transistors, no coupling capacitor Direct coupled D
“select / calculate R so that = …, = …” Design E

2.2 Playbook A: guess, analyse, check

  1. Simplify. Thevenin the base if two resistors or two supplies meet there. Do the collector too if it has two supplies (WS5 Q15).
  2. Guess. If the base-emitter junction is clearly forward biased, guess active. If the base is undriven or reverse biased, guess cut-off.
  3. Analyse (active). Base loop with gives . Then , and the collector loop gives .
  4. Check. Write it in one line: “ = … > 0 and = … > 0.2 V, so active.”
  5. If V, redo in saturation. Set V and keep V. Now and are two unknowns. Write the base loop and the collector loop, and use (not β). Solve them together.
  6. Check saturation. , and . Quote the forced β, .

Shortcut: if the emitter is grounded, the base loop does not involve the collector, so is the same in both attempts and .

2.3 Playbook B: β range

  1. Write (or ) as a function of β using the active model.
  2. For “stays active for all β”: impose V at .
  3. For “always saturated”: impose V with (the edge of saturation) at .
  4. Solve the inequality for the unknown (, , and so on). State which β is the worst case and why.
  5. Sanity check: substitute a standard value at both ends of the range.

2.4 Playbook C: pnp

  1. Draw the real arrows: in at the emitter, and out.
  2. Base-emitter: .
  3. KVL with magnitudes. Each resistor drop is in the arrow direction, so the node the current leaves is the higher one.
  4. Check V and (flowing out).

2.5 Playbook D: two transistors, direct coupled

  1. Find which transistor has a self-contained base loop. Solve it first.
  2. Write the shared node, for example or .
  3. Go through stage 2 using its own β.
  4. If accuracy matters, include in the KCL at the shared node, and say whether you did.
  5. Check both transistors’ states.

2.6 Playbook E: design

  1. List the targets. Use the state they imply: a given V means active.
  2. Get the currents from the targets: and .
  3. Find each resistor from , starting with the loop that has only one unknown.
  4. In divider design, state whether you neglected the divider’s base current, and check .
  5. Choose standard values and re-check.

3. Worked examples

Example 1: pnp, wrong guess then right (WS5 Q10, numbers recomputed)

Given: pnp, base grounded. The emitter goes through 1.5 kΩ to +2.7 V. The collector goes through 20 kΩ to −20 V. β = 100, = 0.7 V, = 0.2 V. Find: the operating mode.

Attempt 1: active. Emitter loop: , so = 1.333 mA. Then = 13.2 µA and = 1.320 mA. Collector loop, from the emitter (0.7 V) down to −20 V: Negative, so the transistor is not active.

Attempt 2: saturation. = 0.2 V. = 1.333 mA is unchanged because the emitter loop does not involve the collector. Check: and mA. The transistor is saturated.

The course solution reaches the same conclusion, but its numbers disagree: it gives V, = 0.925 mA and = 0.405 mA. Substituting into its own loop equation, , gives 1.025 mA. Trust the method, not those printed numbers.

Example 2: collector feedback with a β range (WS5 Q16)

Given: 20 V to = 5 kΩ to the collector. = 120 kΩ from collector to base. = 0.1 kΩ to ground. . Find: at both ends.

The resistor carries . Loop from 20 V through , , and :

β State
80 36.2 µA 2.93 mA 5.34 V 5.04 V active
120 26.2 µA 3.17 mA 4.16 V 3.84 V active

A 50 % increase in β raises by only 8 %, because the feedback through pulls the base current down as the collector voltage falls. The course solution contains the typo “121 × 0.0368”. It should read 121 × 0.0262, and its final 3.168 mA is correct.

Example 3: direct-coupled two-stage DC (Week 5 slides 85 to 88)

Given: 14 V supply. (β = 100) has a 33 kΩ / 10 kΩ divider, = 6.8 kΩ and = 2.2 kΩ. ’s collector drives ’s base directly. (β = 50) has its collector at 14 V and = 1.2 kΩ to ground, so it is an emitter follower. Find: the DC levels.

Stage 1. = 33 ∥ 10 = 7.67 kΩ and = 14(10/43) = 3.26 V. Shared node, ignoring (the lecture’s way): = 6.44 V, = 5.74 V, = 4.78 mA and = 8.26 V. The slide prints 11.17 µA, 6.38 V, 5.68 V, 4.73 mA and 8.32 V. Its denominator 229.2 kΩ should be 229.9 kΩ, which is why its numbers differ slightly.

Including : carries , where . Solving gives = 5.87 V, = 4.30 mA and = 8.83 V. Here 84 µA is not small next to 1.1 mA, so the simplification moves by 0.6 V. In a test, follow the lecture method unless the question asks for more, and add one sentence saying that was neglected.

Check : V, so = 6.44 − 2.47 = 3.97 V > 0.2 V. Active.

Example 4: guaranteed saturation and why “avoid saturation” can be impossible (WS5 Q12)

Given: = 0.01 mA from a current source into the base. = 9 kΩ to 12 V. to ground. Part 2: for which is the transistor always saturated over ?

At the edge of saturation and = 0.2 V: The hardest transistor to saturate is the one with the least collector current, so use = 100: , which gives 2.77 kΩ. This matches the course answer.

The reverse question. Which keeps the transistor active for every β in range? Use = 200: , so kΩ, which is impossible. At β = 200, = 2 mA would need 18 V across the 9 kΩ alone, which is more than the 12 V supply. If the inequality asks for a negative resistor, say that no resistor value works and explain why.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Using in saturation. In saturation the two currents come from two loop equations, and you then check that .
  • Picking the wrong worst-case β. Use to avoid saturation and to guarantee it. WS5 Q13 uses = 200 and gets = 24 µA ( = 3.1 V). That is the threshold at which a β = 200 device starts to saturate. To guarantee saturation for every device in the range you need = 48 µA, which is = 5.5 V. State which one you are giving.
  • Collector feedback: carries , not . Write in the collector term (WS5 Q16, Q19).
  • pnp signs. Writing , or drawing into a pnp base. In practice test Q8 this turns 0.5 V into nonsense.
  • Assuming when the method is invalid. The approximate divider method needs . With it is never valid (see the practice test Q7 comparison in Section 5).
  • Two-stage circuits: forgetting that loads , or adding it with the wrong sign for a pnp. At minimum, say that you neglected it.
  • Bringing in data that does not matter. In practice test Q8, does not enter . Using it anyway signals that you have not understood the circuit.
  • No final check line. Every DC answer ends with “, = … > 0.2 V, so active”, or the saturation equivalent.

PT Q7 (practice test, 10 marks). For the circuit shown on the right, , V, and V. Answer the following questions assuming that the BJT operates in the active state.

Solution

(a) With the base disconnected, the divider runs from +9 V to −12 V:

(b) The drawing: = 2 V in series with = 10 kΩ into the base; a 0.7 V source from base to the grounded emitter; a current source from collector to emitter; = 1.5 kΩ from = 12 V to the collector.

(c) Emitter grounded, so V > 0.2 V, so the active assumption holds. This matches the Test 1 Reference.

The approximate method, compared with the exact one.

Step 1, validity test. The approximate method needs . Here , so kΩ = 300 kΩ. The test fails completely.

Step 2, what happens if you try anyway. The approximate method takes = 2 V, so V. But the emitter is grounded, so must be 0. With no , the “1.3 V across ” step would give . The method has nothing to work with. It relies on to set the current, and this circuit has none.

Step 3, why, with numbers from the exact solution. The base is clamped at = 0.7 V, not 2 V:

  • current in : = 0.553 mA
  • current in : = 0.423 mA
  • base current: 0.553 − 0.423 = 0.130 mA, which agrees with the exact method.

The base current is 24 % of the divider current, so it is far from negligible. That is exactly what the test is designed to detect.

Comparison where the approximate method does give a number (WS5 Q7, the divider-bias circuit from E4): = 54.4 kΩ < = 91 kΩ, so the test fails, but only mildly.

Exact Approximate Error
1.71 mA 1.98 mA () +16 %

For the lecture example (22 V, 39 kΩ / 3.9 kΩ, = 1.5 kΩ, β = 100), where the test passes, the approximate method gives = 0.867 mA and = 12.03 V. The exact method gives 0.838 mA and 12.36 V (slide 33 prints 0.84 mA and 12.34 V). The error is about 3 %.

Conclusion to write: the approximate method is only as good as is large. It cannot be used at all without an emitter resistor, so practice test Q7 must be done with Thevenin.

BJT DC BIAS II (E5)
STATE LOOP: guess -> analyse -> check -> redo
 active: |VBE|=0.7, IC=bIB, IE=(b+1)IB    check IB>0, |VCE|>0.2
 sat:    |VBE|=0.7, |VCE|=0.2, IE=IB+IC   check IB,IC>0, IC<bIB (quote IC/IB)
 cutoff: IB=IC=IE=0                        check |VBE|<0.7
 VCE<=0.2 (negative!) -> sat ;  IB<=0 -> cutoff
 grounded emitter: IB same in both attempts, IC,sat=(VCC-0.2)/RC
 RE present: base & collector loops coupled in sat -> solve 2x2

GENERAL:  IB = (VTh - VBE) / (RTh + (b+1)RE)
 beta range: AVOID sat -> use b_max ; GUARANTEE sat -> use b_min (edge: IC=bIB, VCE=0.2)
 negative R from inequality -> "no value works", explain

COLLECTOR FEEDBACK: IB=(VCC-VBE)/(RF+(b+1)(RC+RE)); RC carries IE
   VCE=VCC-IE(RC+RE)   (slides use b(RC+RE): IC~IE)
EMITTER FOLLOWER: IB=(VEE-VBE)/(RB+(b+1)RE); VCE=VEE-IE*RE
COMMON BASE: IE=(VEE-VBE)/RE; VCB=VCC-IC*RC; VCE=VEE+VCC-IE(RC+RE)

PNP: VB=VE-0.7; IB, IC OUT; IE IN; check VEC>0.2. Draw arrows first.
TWO STAGES: solve stage with own base loop first; shared node;
 npn 2nd stage: RC1 carries IC1+IB2 ; pnp 2nd stage: RC1 carries IC1-IB2
 diode-connected (B=C): always active, drops 0.7 V, its beta irrelevant
APPROX DIVIDER valid only if b*RE >= 10 R2 (never with RE=0)

DESIGN (VDB): VE=0.1VCC; RE=VE/IC; RC=(VCC-VCE-VE)/IC;
 R2 <= b_min RE/10; VB=VE+0.7; R1=R2(VCC-VB)/VB; standard values -> re-check exact
EARLY: iC=IS e^(vBE/VT)(1+vCE/VA); ro=(VA+VCE)/IC ~ VA/IC
